DOCUMENT:
Feasibility Study: Weekly Separate Food Waste Collection
Waste and Environmental Services, Thornbury District Council, October 2026

1. Purpose
Councils in England are required to introduce weekly separate food waste collections for households. This study assesses how Thornbury can deliver the service district-wide from April 2027, based on a six-month pilot, and estimates its costs and savings.

2. The pilot
From January to June 2026, 4,000 households in three wards received a 23-litre outdoor caddy, a 5-litre kitchen caddy and a supply of compostable liners, with collection every week on the same day as their existing bin collection. The pilot wards were chosen to include a mix of houses and flats, and of urban and village streets.

Table 1. Pilot participation by housing type (average weekly set-out, Jan-Jun 2026)
Housing type | Households | Participating households | Participation rate | Food waste per participating household per week
Houses | 3,200 | 2,112 | 66% | 1.9 kg
Flats | 800 | 168 | 21% | 1.4 kg
All | 4,000 | 2,280 | 57% | 1.9 kg

Participation was broadly similar across housing types, which gives us confidence that the service can be rolled out uniformly across the district without a separate approach for flats. Residents' feedback was positive, with 81% of surveyed pilot households rating the service good or very good. Contamination with packaging and other non-food items was low, at under 2% by weight in spot checks carried out at the treatment plant, and missed-collection reports fell steadily after the first month.

3. District-wide projection
Thornbury has 52,000 households, of which about 20% are flats. Applying the pilot's 64% participation rate and 1.9 kg per participating household per week across the district gives about 3,290 tonnes of food waste a year.

4. Treatment
Collected food waste would be taken to Brookfield anaerobic digestion (AD) plant, 14 miles from our depot, at a gate fee of £38 per tonne. Food waste that stays in the residual bin is incinerated at a cost of £112 per tonne. Every tonne diverted therefore saves £74, or around £243,000 a year on the projected tonnage. Brookfield has confirmed that it can offer the Council up to 1,800 tonnes a year of contracted capacity until its planned expansion is completed in 2029. The next nearest AD plant is 46 miles away.

5. Costs
Table 2. Annual cost of district-wide service
Item | Annual cost
Vehicles: six food waste vehicles at £165,000 each, depreciated over seven years | £141,400
Crews: six crews of two at £34,000 per operative | £408,000
Fuel and maintenance | £96,000
Caddies, liners and communications (annualised) | £88,000
Total | £733,400

Against the disposal saving of £243,000, the net annual cost is about £490,000. The Government has indicated that new-burdens funding will be provided for the service; our provisional allocation is £520,000 a year, which would cover the net cost in full.

6. Implementation
Vehicles must be ordered by December 2026 for delivery in March 2027. Caddies would be delivered to all households in March 2027, with a leaflet and a three-month supply of liners. Collections would start in the week of 5 April 2027. Crews will be recruited from February 2027 and trained on the new vehicles during March. A dedicated phone line and web page will handle caddy requests and missed collections during the first three months of the service.

7. Recommendation
The pilot demonstrates strong participation and resident satisfaction, and the service can be delivered on a uniform basis across the district. With treatment at Brookfield and new-burdens funding, the service is fully funded. We recommend that Cabinet approve the district-wide roll-out from April 2027 and authorise the vehicle order.

KEY (three known flaws):
1. [inconsistency] at: "Applying the pilot's 64% participation rate" -- Table 1 gives the pilot participation rate as 57% overall (66% houses, 21% flats); the projection applies a '64%' pilot participation rate. (64% x 52,000 x 1.9 kg x 52 = about 3,290 t; at 57% it would be about 2,930 t.)
2. [misread_evidence] at: "Participation was broadly similar across housing types" -- Table 1 shows participation of 66% in houses but only 21% in flats, a very large difference. The claim misreads the table, and the conclusion that a uniform service needs no separate approach for flats rests on it.
3. [missing_consideration] at: "Every tonne diverted therefore saves £74, or around £243,000 a year on the projected tonnage." -- The saving assumes all projected tonnage (about 3,290 t) goes to Brookfield at £38/t, but the document states Brookfield can take only 1,800 t a year until 2029 and the next plant is 46 miles away. The excess tonnage's treatment and haulage cost is never addressed, though the 'fully funded' conclusion depends on it.

REVIEW:
# Review: Feasibility Study, Weekly Separate Food Waste Collection (Thornbury)

**What it proposes.** Roll out weekly food waste collection to all 52,000 households from April 2027, as a single service for all housing types, based on a six-month pilot. It projects 3,290 tonnes a year, a disposal saving of £243,000, a net cost of about £490,000, and says the provisional £520,000 new-burdens allocation covers this in full.

**Verdict.** The service is a legal requirement, so the real question is how to deliver it, not whether. On that, the study's own tables contradict three of its main conclusions:

1. Flats' participation did **not** hold up.
2. The projection uses a participation rate that appears nowhere in the pilot data.
3. Brookfield can take only about 55–63% of the projected tonnage.

Once these are corrected, the service is **not** fully funded even in the best case. Ordering the vehicles is probably still right. The funding and flats claims need correcting before Cabinet relies on them.

---

## 1. What checks out

- **Table 1 rates.** 2,112/3,200 = 66%, 168/800 = 21%, 2,280/4,000 = 57%. The combined yield rounds correctly to 1.9 kg.
- **Table 2 sums.** Vehicles 6 × £165,000 ÷ 7 = £141,400. Crews 12 × £34,000 = £408,000. Total £733,400. Net £490,400.
- **The projection arithmetic, on its stated inputs.** 52,000 × 64% × 1.9 kg × 52 weeks ≈ 3,290 t. The saving of £74 × 3,290 ≈ £243,000.
- **The pilot design.** Mixed wards with the same share of flats as the district (20%), weekly measurement, and contamination checked at the plant are all good practice.

---

## 2. Flats: the pilot shows the opposite of the conclusion

The text says "participation was broadly similar across housing types." The table shows **66% for houses and 21% for flats**, so flats participated at about a third of the rate of houses. They also produced less food waste per participating household (1.4 kg vs 1.9 kg).

The pilot is evidence that the standard service **does not work well for flats**. That is a common finding: flats usually need communal bins, a different collection approach and targeted communications. The case for "a single, simple service" is the opposite of what the data support, and the Recommendation repeats it. The flats approach needs its own design and budget.

---

## 3. The projection uses the wrong participation rate

Section 3 applies **64%**. The pilot measured **57%** overall, and the district has the same share of flats (20%) as the pilot. Using the pilot's own figures:

| | Households | Participation | kg/week | Tonnes/year |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Houses | 41,600 | 66% | 1.9 | about 2,710 |
| Flats | 10,400 | 21% | 1.4 | about 160 |
| **Total** | 52,000 | | | **about 2,870** |

That is about 13% below the study's 3,290 t. The disposal saving falls to at most about **£212,000** if all of it went to Brookfield.

Pilot participation may also not hold district-wide: pilots get extra attention and novelty. The projection should show a range, not a single figure.

---

## 4. Brookfield can't take it all

Section 4 says Brookfield will offer **up to 1,800 tonnes a year until 2029**, but the study projects 3,290 t. Even the corrected 2,870 t leaves about **1,070 t a year** with nowhere costed to go.

- **The saving is overstated.** Brookfield capacity saves at most 1,800 × £74 = **£133,200**.
- **The overflow has no cost attached.** The next plant is 46 miles away, with an unknown gate fee and much longer journeys. Burning the overflow instead would save nothing, and would undermine the point of collecting food waste separately.
- **"Treatment is local" is true only for the first 1,800 tonnes.**
- **The capacity isn't secured yet.** Brookfield has "confirmed it can offer" it. Nothing is under contract.

---

## 5. "Fully funded" doesn't hold

| Scenario | Disposal saving | Net cost | vs £520,000 allocation |
|---|---|---|---|
| Study as written | £243,000 | £490,400 | £29,600 under |
| Corrected tonnage, all diverted at £74/t (not possible at Brookfield) | £212,400 | £521,000 | **£1,000 over** |
| Corrected tonnage, overflow saves nothing | £133,200 | £600,200 | **about £80,000 over** |

Even before adding the costs missing from §6, the corrected figures exceed the allocation.

The allocation itself is **provisional**: the government has "indicated" it. The study had a margin of only £30,000, so any shortfall in confirmed funding leaves the Council paying the difference.

---

## 6. Likely missing costs

- **Cover for absence.** Twelve operatives with no allowance for holidays or sickness. Typical cover adds 15–20% to crew costs.
- **What "£34,000 per operative" includes.** Is it salary only, or does it include employer National Insurance and pension? If salary only, crew costs are understated by roughly 25–30%.
- **Supervision, the phone line and web page, and capital financing** on the vehicles are not costed.
- **Overflow haulage** and any transfer station or bulking point are not costed.
- **Cash flow.** Caddies for 52,000 households are paid for up front in 2027-28, but the cost is shown annualised.
- **Rounds.** The study doesn't show that six vehicles can serve about 10,400 households a day including trips to Brookfield. It may be achievable, but the route modelling should be included.

---

## 7. Timetable and legal deadline

- **Check the legal deadline.** My understanding is that "Simpler Recycling" requires English councils to collect household food waste weekly from **31 March 2026**, with transitional arrangements for some councils. A start in April 2027 is a year after that. The study should state whether Thornbury has a transitional arrangement. If it doesn't, the Council is already behind, which strengthens the case for ordering vehicles now.
- **There is no slack in the timetable.** Vehicles are delivered in March, crews are trained in March on those vehicles, and collections start on 5 April. A slip in vehicle delivery delays the start. Recruitment from February also leaves little time if HGV drivers are hard to find. Add contingency, such as hired vehicles.
- **Contract timing.** The Brookfield contract should be signed before the vehicle order is committed.

---

## 8. Smaller points

- **Satisfaction.** 81% of *surveyed* households: the study doesn't give the survey size or response rate. People who took part in the pilot are more likely to respond and more likely to be positive.
- **Seasonal coverage.** Six months from January to June misses summer and the run-up to Christmas, when food waste volumes differ. That is another reason to give a range.
- **Contamination.** Under 2% in the pilot is good. Expect it to be higher at scale, particularly from communal bins at flats.

---

## 9. What the study claims vs what the evidence supports

| Claim | Status |
|---|---|
| Participation held across houses and flats | **Contradicted** by Table 1 (66% vs 21%) |
| About 3,290 t a year | **Overstated.** The pilot data give about 2,870 t |
| Treatment local at Brookfield | **Only for 1,800 t a year until 2029**, and not yet contracted |
| Net cost about £490,000 | **Understated.** About £521,000–£600,000 before missing costs |
| Fully covered by £520,000 | **Not supported.** Allocation is provisional and corrected costs exceed it |
| Cost lines complete | **Gaps** in crew cover, on-costs, overflow and financing |
| Strong participation, high satisfaction among houses | Supported, with the survey caveat |

---

## Bottom line

**Approve the vehicle order.** The service is a legal requirement and the vehicles take time to arrive. Don't present the roll-out as fully funded or as a single service for everyone. Before go-live, the paper should:

1. Recalculate tonnage at 57% participation and show a range.
2. Design and cost a separate approach for flats.
3. Secure and cost treatment for the tonnage Brookfield can't take.
4. Add the missing cost lines and present the funding gap honestly.
5. Confirm the legal deadline position.

**Still open:** the size of the funding gap, which depends on the overflow treatment cost and on confirmation of the new-burdens allocation; and the participation rate the full roll-out will achieve.
